Changing only -var-file does not change backend state. Use independent roots, explicit backend configurations and verified AWS identities.

HCL / terminal — example environment values
# environments/dev/terraform.tfvars
# instance_type = "t3.micro"
# replica_count = 1
# environment   = "dev"

# environments/prod/terraform.tfvars
# instance_type = "m7i.large"
# replica_count = 3
# environment   = "prod"

# Execute from the appropriate root directory:
# terraform -chdir=environments/dev plan -out=tfplan
# Each root must use its own backend and scoped AWS role.

Final interview answer

We keep the common infrastructure implementation in reusable modules and define environment-specific settings in separate roots or approved variable files. Dev might use smaller instance types and fewer replicas, while Production uses additional capacity and stronger availability settings. Each environment has its own backend state key and scoped AWS role, so using the same modules does not mean sharing state. I test module changes in lower environments and generate a separate reviewed production plan before promoting the version.

074What are Terraform provider aliases, and how do you use them to deploy resources across multiple AWS regions?
HCL · choose the region via provider alias
provider "aws" {
  region = "ap-south-1"
}
provider "aws" {
  alias  = "dr"
  region = "us-east-1"
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "dr" {
  provider = aws.dr
  bucket   = var.dr_bucket_name
}

Final interview answer

Provider aliases allow us to configure multiple instances of the same provider, such as aws.primary for Mumbai and aws.dr for another region. I assign a resource to the appropriate provider using the provider meta-argument, or pass an aliased provider to a child module using the providers map. Terraform then manages each resource in the region configured for that provider instance. I make provider selection explicit when provisioning multi-region infrastructure so that resources are not accidentally created in the default region.

075How do you deploy resources into multiple AWS accounts using Terraform and IAM assume-role configuration?
HCL · cross-account provider guard
provider "aws" {
  alias               = "prod"
  region              = "ap-south-1"
  allowed_account_ids = [var.production_account_id]
  assume_role { role_arn = var.production_role_arn }
}

Final interview answer

I start with an approved identity that can assume scoped roles in the target AWS accounts. Each Terraform provider instance can use an assume_role configuration with the appropriate role ARN and region, and I pass those provider configurations to the relevant modules. In practice, I often use separate roots and state per account to keep the blast radius and access permissions clear. Before planning or applying, I verify the identity and use account guardrails such as allowed_account_ids to prevent unintended deployments.

State, Backend and Import — Intermediate

076How do you configure an Amazon S3 remote backend for Terraform?

The backend bucket must exist before initialization of the dependent root. Bootstrap and protect it separately; do not destroy the state bucket as part of application cleanup.

HCL · backend.tf (pre-created bucket; Terraform >= 1.10)
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10.0"
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "replace-with-state-bucket"
    key          = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}

Implementation / troubleshooting sequence

  1. Bootstrap a dedicated state bucket with versioning, encryption, nonpublic access and IAM/KMS controls.
  2. Define a unique state key and supported locking in backend.tf; verify the approved identity.
  3. Run terraform init using the intended backend; migrate only under change control.
  4. Inspect the expected state, test lock behavior in a safe environment and verify a clean or intended plan.

Final interview answer

I first create a dedicated, private S3 state bucket through an approved bootstrap process and enable versioning, encryption and appropriate public-access restrictions. In the application root, I configure the S3 backend with the bucket name, region, unique state key and native locking where supported. The CI or developer identity must have scoped S3 and, if used, KMS access for state and lock operations. After terraform init, I verify that the intended state is available before allowing infrastructure changes.

077How do you configure Terraform state locking using S3 native lockfiles or the older DynamoDB-based approach? What is the difference?
FeatureS3 native lockfileLegacy DynamoDB locking
Configurationuse_lockfile = truedynamodb_table = "terraform-lock"
Lock storageState key plus .tflock objectDynamoDB item with LockID
Client supportTerraform 1.10+ compatible clientsOlder compatible clients
PermissionsS3 GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject on lockDynamoDB table read/write/delete and describe
StatusSupported native S3 approachDeprecated; coordinate migration
ImportantDo not manually delete active lockDo not remove table until all writers migrated

Native S3 locking is opt-in. On compatible clients, use_lockfile creates a lock object next to the state. See the official S3 backend documentation for exact IAM scope and migration details.

HCL — native locking and legacy configuration
# Modern S3 backend (existing private bucket; Terraform >= 1.10)
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "replace-with-state-bucket"
    key          = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}

# Legacy configuration: inside the S3 backend block,
# dynamodb_table = "terraform-lock"
# Table partition key: LockID (String)
# During a reviewed transition both options can coexist.

Reference: S3 backend, state locking, migration and IAM permissions

Final interview answer

For modern Terraform versions supporting native S3 locking, I enable use_lockfile in the S3 backend and grant the required permissions on the corresponding .tflock object. Older configurations use a DynamoDB table with a string partition key named LockID, referenced by dynamodb_table; this approach is now deprecated. During migration, compatible clients and backend settings must be coordinated, and both settings may be configured together during the transition. I verify every state writer uses compatible locking before retiring the older mechanism, because preventing concurrent writes matters more than merely changing the backend syntax.

078How do you migrate an existing local Terraform state file to an S3 remote backend?
CLI · controlled migration (freeze writers first)
umask 077
terraform state pull > /secure/path/pre-migration.tfstate
# Add the reviewed remote backend configuration.
terraform init -migrate-state
terraform state list
terraform plan

Implementation / troubleshooting sequence

  1. Stop writers and record the current state identity and lineage; make a protected local backup.
  2. Bootstrap and verify remote storage and lock permissions.
  3. Add the approved backend block and run terraform init -migrate-state, reviewing prompts.
  4. Inspect the remote state and run a fresh plan before releasing the change window.

Final interview answer

I first stop all operations against the existing state and make a protected backup of the local state. After creating and securing the remote backend, I add its configuration and run terraform init -migrate-state from the correct root, reviewing the migration prompt. I check that the remote state has the expected resources, lineage and outputs and run a fresh plan to confirm that it does not propose unexpected creation or destruction. Only after verification do I remove unnecessary local copies according to our security policy and allow the team to resume deployments.

079How do you share infrastructure outputs between two independent Terraform projects using terraform_remote_state?

When the consumer must not see full state, publish a nonsecret interface through SSM Parameter Store, DNS or another approved API instead.

HCL · reading approved remote state output
data "terraform_remote_state" "network" {
  backend = "s3"
  config = {
    bucket = "approved-state-bucket"
    key    = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "ap-south-1"
  }
}
output "network_vpc_id" {
  value = data.terraform_remote_state.network.outputs.vpc_id
}
# Access grants visibility of full state, not only outputs.

Final interview answer

An independent infrastructure stack can expose selected values as root module outputs, for example a VPC ID and private subnet IDs. Another root can use the terraform_remote_state data source to read those outputs from the approved backend. However, access to remote-state outputs usually requires permission to read the underlying state snapshot, which may contain more sensitive information. Where stronger isolation is required, I publish only the necessary values through a dedicated interface such as SSM Parameter Store rather than giving another team full state access.

080Explain Terraform state management commands, including state list, state show, state mv, state rm, state pull and state push.
CommandPurpose / risk
state listList managed and data resource addresses
state show ADDRESSDisplay recorded resource details
state mv OLD NEWChange address mapping
state rm ADDRESSForget mapping; does not delete AWS object
state pullRead state snapshot; sensitive output
state push FILEOverwrite backend state subject to checks; recovery only

The examples for state-changing commands are commented deliberately. Never execute them without verifying the state, exact address, backup and absence of competing writers.

Terminal — example commands
terraform state list
terraform state show aws_instance.web
umask 077
# Backup only to an authorized protected location:
# terraform state pull > /secure/path/state-backup.tfstate
# Review address mappings and ownership before any mutation:
# terraform state mv -dry-run aws_instance.web aws_instance.api
# terraform state rm -dry-run aws_instance.web
# terraform state mv aws_instance.web aws_instance.api
# terraform state rm aws_instance.web
# terraform state push /secure/path/verified.tfstate  # Recovery only

Final interview answer

I use state list and state show to inspect managed resource addresses and the information Terraform currently records for them. state mv changes the address mapping without directly changing the cloud object, and state rm removes the mapping without deleting that object. state pull retrieves a state snapshot, while state push writes a snapshot to the configured backend and is normally reserved for carefully controlled recovery. Before any state-changing operation, I verify the correct environment, stop concurrent writers, protect a backup and inspect the resulting plan.

081What is Terraform import, and when do we need to import existing AWS resources?
Terminal — example commands
# Verify existing bucket and management ownership first.
# Declare matching resource aws_s3_bucket.legacy in configuration.
# After approval:
# terraform import aws_s3_bucket.legacy "$EXISTING_BUCKET"
terraform plan

Final interview answer

Terraform import brings an existing infrastructure object under Terraform management by associating it with a resource address in state. I use it when a resource was created manually or by another process and we want Terraform to become its authorized owner without creating a duplicate. The destination configuration must describe the actual object, and the provider must support importing it. After importing, I review a fresh plan and align the configuration so that Terraform does not unexpectedly modify or replace the resource.

082What is the difference between terraform import and the declarative import block? How do you import an existing EC2 instance?
terraform import commandDeclarative import block
Direct state associationVersion-controlled import intent
terraform import aws_instance.web i-...import { to = aws_instance.web; id = ... } conceptually
Normally write destination configuration firstPlan can review proposed import and may generate configuration
Executed immediately via CLIExecuted during approved apply
Review subsequent planReview import and other changes before apply

Import is not a configuration generator for every resource. Verify the actual resource fields, provider import support and unique ownership; generated code requires review.

HCL — EC2 import (replace ID and match configuration)
# Destination configuration — match the actual EC2 settings
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = var.existing_ami_id
  instance_type = var.existing_instance_type
  subnet_id     = var.existing_subnet_id
  # Include all relevant existing settings before applying.
}
# CLI alternative: terraform import aws_instance.web i-REPLACE

# Declarative alternative (do not run both methods):
import {
  to = aws_instance.web
  id = "i-REPLACE_WITH_EXISTING_ID"
}
Terminal — example commands
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID"
terraform plan -out=import.tfplan
terraform show import.tfplan
# Apply only after confirming import and all other changes.

Reference: Importing existing infrastructure

Implementation / troubleshooting sequence

  1. Find the EC2 instance ID and verify its account, region and existing owner.
  2. Write the destination resource configuration to match the instance; do not duplicate ownership.
  3. Choose CLI import or a declarative import block, and review the plan.
  4. After import, inspect the state and verify that no unexpected create or replacement is proposed.

Final interview answer

The terraform import CLI command associates a real object with a specified address directly in state and usually requires the corresponding resource configuration to be written first. A declarative import block allows us to record the import in configuration, preview the operation in a plan and execute it through the normal approved apply workflow. For an EC2 instance, I confirm the exact instance ID, account and existing ownership before importing it into aws_instance.web. I then compare the configuration against the actual instance and review the plan for any unintended changes.

083What are Terraform moved and removed blocks, and how do they help manage infrastructure refactoring?
moved blockremoved block
Maps old address to new addressDeclares end of Terraform ownership
Preserves object when configuration remains compatibledestroy = false preserves underlying object
Useful for resource rename or module refactorUseful for approved handoff
Review plan for move actionsReview plan for removal without destruction
HCL — moved and removed blocks (separate operations)
# Rename or move an existing object in the same state:
moved {
  from = aws_instance.web
  to   = module.compute.aws_instance.web
}

# Independent example: approved handoff of a bucket.
# Remove the previous resource declaration and add:
removed {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.legacy
  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}

Reference: Refactoring module addresses

Final interview answer

A moved block tells Terraform that an existing resource or module address has changed, so Terraform can preserve the underlying object rather than treating the rename as a deletion and creation. A removed block declares that an object should leave Terraform management, and with lifecycle destroy = false it can be forgotten without deleting the actual infrastructure. These blocks let us record important state transitions in version-controlled code rather than relying only on manual state commands. I verify the plan and confirm ownership before using them because incorrect addresses or a removal configured to destroy can have serious consequences.

084What is Terraform refresh? What is the difference between a normal plan and a refresh-only plan?
Normal planRefresh-only plan
Reads remote objects then plans desired configuration changesPlans only updates to state and root outputs
Can propose create, update, replace or deleteDoes not plan normal infrastructure reconciliation
terraform planterraform plan -refresh-only
Use for regular changesUse to review observed external changes
Approved apply may change resourcesApproved refresh-only apply updates recorded state

Do not apply refresh-only blindly just to hide a manual change. It updates the record, not the desired configuration.

Terminal · commands
terraform plan -refresh-only
terraform plan

Reference: Normal and refresh-only planning modes

Final interview answer

Refreshing means reading the actual managed resource information through the providers and updating Terraform's understanding of the infrastructure. A normal plan usually refreshes the information and then calculates changes required to reach the configuration. A refresh-only plan focuses on updating the recorded state and outputs to match observed remote objects, rather than proposing infrastructure reconciliation. I review refresh-only changes before applying them and prefer this workflow over the older terraform refresh command, which updates state without the same normal review step.

085What is Terraform drift, and how do you detect infrastructure changes made manually through the AWS Console?
Terminal · commands
terraform plan -refresh-only
terraform plan -out=tfplan

Final interview answer

Drift occurs when the actual infrastructure differs from the configuration or previously recorded expectations, for example when someone adds a security group rule manually. A normal Terraform plan with refresh enabled can reveal those differences and show whether Terraform would change the resource to match the code. I also review refresh-only plans and CloudTrail events where appropriate to understand what changed and why. We then decide whether to restore the approved configuration or update the code through review to adopt a legitimate operational change.

086What is the difference between terraform taint, terraform untaint and the recommended -replace option?
taintuntaint-replace option
Mark instance for replacementRemove taint markRequest replacement in reviewed plan
Changes state markerChanges state markerDoes not need separate taint operation
Deprecated workflow for replacementLegacy taint recoveryterraform plan -replace=ADDRESS
Later apply may replace itDoes not reverse completed replacementReview saved plan before apply
Terminal — example commands
# Preview a replacement with modern Terraform:
terraform plan -replace=aws_instance.web -out=replace.tfplan
terraform show replace.tfplan
# After explicit review and approval: terraform apply replace.tfplan
# Legacy commands (not recommended for routine replacements):
# terraform taint aws_instance.web
# terraform untaint aws_instance.web

Final interview answer

The older terraform taint command marks a managed resource instance in state for replacement during a future apply, and untaint removes that mark. For current workflows, I prefer terraform plan -replace=RESOURCE_ADDRESS because it expresses the replacement directly in a plan that can be reviewed and saved. This avoids leaving a separate persistent taint mark that another engineer might apply unintentionally. I only request replacement after checking dependent resources, downtime and data-retention implications.

Practical AWS Infrastructure Provisioning — Intermediate

087Can you write Terraform code to create a complete VPC with public and private subnets, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway and route tables?

Illustrative three-tier VPC: two public subnets, two application subnets and two database subnets. NAT is optional for development; enable it only when approved. NAT gateways and Elastic IPs may incur charges.

HCL — VPC and routes (combine the two excerpts in one root)
variable "azs" {
  type    = list(string)
  default = ["ap-south-1a", "ap-south-1b"]
}
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = "10.0.0.0/16"
  enable_dns_support   = true
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
}
resource "aws_subnet" "public" {
  for_each          = { for i, az in var.azs : az => i }
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = each.key
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(aws_vpc.main.cidr_block, 8, each.value)
}
resource "aws_subnet" "app" {
  for_each          = { for i, az in var.azs : az => i }
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = each.key
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(aws_vpc.main.cidr_block, 8, 10 + each.value)
}
resource "aws_subnet" "db" {
  for_each          = { for i, az in var.azs : az => i }
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = each.key
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(aws_vpc.main.cidr_block, 8, 20 + each.value)
}
resource "aws_internet_gateway" "main" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}
resource "aws_route_table" "public" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
  route {
    cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
    gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.main.id
  }
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "public" {
  for_each       = aws_subnet.public
  subnet_id      = each.value.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.public.id
}
# Continue with routes.tf below for private routing.
# For ALB/app/DB security-group rules, see Q88.
HCL — VPC and routes (combine the two excerpts in one root)
variable "enable_nat" {
  type    = bool
  default = false # NAT gateways incur charges
}
resource "aws_eip" "nat" {
  for_each = var.enable_nat ? aws_subnet.public : {}
  domain   = "vpc"
}
resource "aws_nat_gateway" "app" {
  for_each      = aws_eip.nat
  allocation_id = each.value.id
  subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public[each.key].id
  depends_on    = [aws_internet_gateway.main]
}
resource "aws_route_table" "app" {
  for_each = aws_subnet.app
  vpc_id   = aws_vpc.main.id
}
resource "aws_route" "app_egress" {
  for_each               = aws_nat_gateway.app
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.app[each.key].id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = each.value.id
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "app" {
  for_each       = aws_subnet.app
  subnet_id      = each.value.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.app[each.key].id
}
resource "aws_route_table" "db" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}
resource "aws_route_table_association" "db" {
  for_each       = aws_subnet.db
  subnet_id      = each.value.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.db.id
}
HCL — network outputs
# outputs.tf
output "vpc_id" {
  value = aws_vpc.main.id
}
output "public_subnet_ids" {
  value = [for s in aws_subnet.public : s.id]
}
output "private_subnet_ids" {
  value = [for s in aws_subnet.app : s.id]
}
output "database_subnet_ids" {
  value = [for s in aws_subnet.db : s.id]
}
Terminal — example commands
terraform init
terraform validate
# NAT defaults to disabled; enable only when approved:
terraform plan -var='enable_nat=true' -out=network.tfplan
terraform show network.tfplan
# Approved apply: terraform apply network.tfplan
# Verify route associations and the output IDs in AWS.

Implementation / troubleshooting sequence

  1. Confirm approved CIDR ranges, AZs, subnet sizes and routing requirements.
  2. Create the VPC and public/private subnets, Internet Gateway and route tables.
  3. Enable zonal NAT gateways where approved and associate private subnet routes; keep DB subnets isolated as needed.
  4. Review the plan and verify routes, output IDs and subnet design in AWS.

Final interview answer

I start with the approved VPC CIDR and divide it into nonoverlapping public and private subnets across the required Availability Zones. I attach an Internet Gateway for public routing, provision NAT capacity when private workloads require outbound internet access and associate each subnet with the correct route table. I normally expose the VPC and subnet IDs as module outputs so compute and EKS stacks can consume them. Before deployment, I verify the routing design, security controls, address capacity and NAT costs, and confirm all resources in AWS after the approved apply.

088Can you write Terraform code to create security groups that allow an Application Load Balancer to communicate with EC2 instances and an RDS database?

Example traffic path: Internet HTTPS → ALB:443 → EC2:8080 → PostgreSQL:5432. The database security group permits only the application security group. Other required egress (patching, endpoints, DNS) must be reviewed separately.

HCL · security-groups.tf (network VPC ID input required)
resource "aws_security_group" "alb" {
  name   = "app-alb"
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
}
resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  name   = "app-private"
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
}
resource "aws_security_group" "db" {
  name   = "app-db"
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "https" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  cidr_ipv4         = "0.0.0.0/0"
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "alb_to_app" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.app.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 8080
  to_port                      = 8080
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "app_to_db" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.db.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 5432
  to_port                      = 5432
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "alb_to_app" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.alb.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 8080
  to_port                      = 8080
}
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "app_to_db" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.app.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.db.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 5432
  to_port                      = 5432
}
Terminal — example commands
# After applying the approved security group configuration:
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids "$ALB_SG" "$APP_SG" "$DB_SG"
# Verify allowed HTTPS and app-to-DB traffic from authorized test clients.

Final interview answer

I configure a security group for each application tier rather than opening all ports to the VPC or internet. The ALB accepts approved HTTPS traffic, the EC2 application security group permits the application port only from the ALB security group, and the RDS group allows the database port only from the application group. I also verify outbound requirements and avoid direct public access to the database. After applying the configuration, I test the expected traffic flow and confirm that unauthorized access paths remain blocked.

089How do you provision EC2 instances using the latest approved AMI retrieved through a Terraform data source?

Using most_recent = true can introduce unexpected image replacement when a new AMI matches the filters. Prefer an approved release parameter or pin when controlled upgrades are needed.

HCL · EC2 example (existing subnet and SG required)
variable "subnet_id" { type = string }
variable "security_group_id" { type = string }
data "aws_ami" "linux" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["amazon"]
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["al2023-ami-*-x86_64"]
  }
}
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami                         = data.aws_ami.linux.id
  instance_type               = "t3.micro"
  subnet_id                   = var.subnet_id
  vpc_security_group_ids      = [var.security_group_id]
  associate_public_ip_address = false
  root_block_device { encrypted = true }
  metadata_options { http_tokens = "required" }
  tags = { Name = "web-dev" }
}
HCL — approved AMI release via SSM (excerpt)
# Alternatively, resolve a platform-owned approved AMI parameter:
data "aws_ssm_parameter" "approved_ami" {
  name = "/platform/approved-ami/al2023/x86_64"
}
# Use data.aws_ssm_parameter.approved_ami.value for ami.
# The parameter must exist in this region and contain an approved AMI ID.

Final interview answer

I use an aws_ami data source with an approved owner and filters that identify the image family our application supports. The instance resource references the returned AMI ID, which avoids hardcoding an unrelated or region-specific image ID. If we select the most recent approved image automatically, I review the plan carefully because a new matching AMI can require instance replacement. For production, we may pin a verified AMI release or consume an approved image parameter to control when upgrades occur.

090How do you create a Launch Template, Auto Scaling Group and Application Load Balancer using Terraform?

Example assumes the networking, security groups, certificate and application bootstrap already exist. The app must actually listen on the target port and serve the configured health check.

HCL — Launch Template, ALB, ASG and scaling (required inputs declared separately)
# Prerequisites: declare approved inputs for VPC, subnets, SGs, AMI,
# EC2 instance profile, ACM certificate ARN and bootstrap file.
resource "aws_launch_template" "app" {
  name_prefix   = "payment-app-"
  image_id      = var.approved_ami_id
  instance_type = var.instance_type
  vpc_security_group_ids = [var.app_security_group_id]
  iam_instance_profile {
    name = var.instance_profile_name
  }
  metadata_options {
    http_tokens = "required"
  }
  user_data = filebase64("${path.module}/bootstrap.sh")
}
resource "aws_lb" "app" {
  name               = "payment-alb"
  internal           = false
  load_balancer_type = "application"
  subnets            = var.public_subnet_ids
  security_groups    = [var.alb_security_group_id]
}
resource "aws_lb_target_group" "app" {
  name_prefix = "pay-"
  port        = 8080
  protocol    = "HTTP"
  vpc_id      = var.vpc_id
  target_type = "instance"
  health_check {
    path    = "/health"
    matcher = "200"
  }
}
resource "aws_lb_listener" "https" {
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.app.arn
  port              = 443
  protocol          = "HTTPS"
  certificate_arn   = var.certificate_arn
  default_action {
    type             = "forward"
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.app.arn
  }
}
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "app" {
  min_size                  = 2
  max_size                  = 6
  desired_capacity          = 2
  vpc_zone_identifier       = var.private_subnet_ids
  target_group_arns         = [aws_lb_target_group.app.arn]
  health_check_type         = "ELB"
  health_check_grace_period = 180
  launch_template {
    id      = aws_launch_template.app.id
    version = aws_launch_template.app.latest_version
  }
  instance_refresh {
    strategy = "Rolling"
    preferences {
      min_healthy_percentage = 100
      instance_warmup        = 180
    }
  }
  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [desired_capacity] # only if scaling owns this field
  }
}
resource "aws_autoscaling_policy" "cpu" {
  name                   = "payment-cpu"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.app.name
  policy_type            = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  target_tracking_configuration {
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"
    }
    target_value = 60
  }
}
Terminal — example commands
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$TARGET_GROUP_ARN"
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names "$ASG_NAME"
curl --fail --show-error "https://$APP_HOST/health"

Implementation / troubleshooting sequence

  1. Confirm approved networking, ALB TLS certificate, application listener and health endpoint.
  2. Create the Launch Template and ALB target group/listener.
  3. Create ASG across private subnets, attach the target group and configure scaling and health checks.
  4. Apply the reviewed plan and verify healthy target registration and application responses.

Final interview answer

I create a Launch Template with the approved AMI, instance type, security groups and instance profile, then use it in an Auto Scaling Group deployed across eligible private subnets. I configure an ALB, target group and listener and attach the target group to the ASG so healthy instances can receive traffic. I set minimum, desired and maximum capacity based on application requirements and configure health checks and scaling policies where needed. The deployment plan must also consider instance refresh behavior, availability during updates and sufficient capacity across zones.

091How do you provision an RDS database in private subnets using Terraform with backups, encryption and deletion protection?

Do not use skip_final_snapshot = true for an important production database unless the approved recovery policy explicitly permits it. Confirm supported engine and instance versions.

HCL — private RDS (additional inputs and compatible engine version required)
resource "aws_db_subnet_group" "app" {
  name       = "payment-db"
  subnet_ids = var.database_subnet_ids
}
resource "aws_db_instance" "app" {
  identifier                  = "payment-db"
  engine                      = "postgres"
  engine_version              = var.approved_postgres_version
  instance_class              = var.db_instance_class
  allocated_storage           = 50
  storage_type                = "gp3"
  storage_encrypted           = true
  username                    = "appadmin"
  manage_master_user_password = true
  db_subnet_group_name        = aws_db_subnet_group.app.name
  vpc_security_group_ids      = [var.database_security_group_id]
  publicly_accessible         = false
  multi_az                    = true
  backup_retention_period     = 7
  deletion_protection         = true
  skip_final_snapshot         = false
  final_snapshot_identifier   = var.approved_final_snapshot_identifier
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}
output "db_endpoint" {
  value = aws_db_instance.app.endpoint
}
Terminal — example commands
terraform plan -out=database.tfplan
terraform show database.tfplan
# After approved provisioning:
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier payment-db
# Confirm approved application network can reach the DB; do not print secrets.

Final interview answer

I create a DB subnet group using approved private subnets and configure a database security group that allows access only from the required application tier. In the RDS resource, I configure the engine, instance class, storage encryption, backups, deletion protection and availability requirements. I use an approved secret-management approach, such as an RDS-managed master password where supported, to avoid passing plaintext database passwords through configuration. Before applying changes, I check the plan for any replacement, and I verify connectivity, backup configuration and the database endpoint after provisioning.

092How do you create IAM roles, IAM policies and EC2 instance profiles using Terraform?
HCL · EC2 role and instance profile excerpt
resource "aws_iam_role" "app" {
  name = "app-ec2-role"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect    = "Allow"
      Action    = "sts:AssumeRole"
      Principal = { Service = "ec2.amazonaws.com" }
    }]
  })
}
resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "read" {
  name = "read-app-config"
  role = aws_iam_role.app.id
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect   = "Allow"
      Action   = ["s3:GetObject"]
      Resource = "${var.config_bucket_arn}/config/*"
    }]
  })
}
resource "aws_iam_instance_profile" "app" {
  name = "app-profile"
  role = aws_iam_role.app.name
}
Terminal — example commands
# Attach the instance profile to EC2 or a launch template:
# iam_instance_profile = aws_iam_instance_profile.app.name
# From an authorized application instance, verify:
aws sts get-caller-identity

Final interview answer

I first define the role's trust policy, which specifies which service or identity is allowed to assume it. Then I create or attach the permissions policy that grants only the actions and resources required by the application. For EC2, I create an instance profile that contains the role and reference that profile in the EC2 or Launch Template configuration. I verify that the instance receives temporary credentials for the expected role and can perform only its authorized AWS operations.

093How do you provision an S3 bucket with lifecycle policies, bucket policies and public access restrictions?
HCL · private S3 bucket (globally unique name required)
variable "unique_bucket_name" { type = string }
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "artifacts" {
  bucket = var.unique_bucket_name
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "artifacts" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "artifacts" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  versioning_configuration { status = "Enabled" }
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "artifacts" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm = "AES256"
    }
  }
}
HCL · lifecycle example (bucket/versioning from Q33)
resource "aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration" "artifacts" {
  bucket     = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket_versioning.artifacts]
  rule {
    id     = "expire-old-versions"
    status = "Enabled"
    filter {}
    noncurrent_version_expiration {
      noncurrent_days = 90
    }
  }
}
# Retention must meet legal and business requirements.
HCL — bucket policy example
# Additional bucket policy — enforce TLS.
resource "aws_s3_bucket_policy" "tls_only" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Sid       = "DenyInsecureTransport"
      Effect    = "Deny"
      Principal = "*"
      Action    = "s3:*"
      Resource = [
        aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.arn,
        "${aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.arn}/*"
      ]
      Condition = {
        Bool = { "aws:SecureTransport" = "false" }
      }
    }]
  })
}
# Keep all bucket policy statements in the single owning resource.
# Add separately reviewed authorized principal access where needed.

Final interview answer

I create the S3 bucket with the approved name, tags and ownership settings, then configure versioning, encryption and public access blocking as separate resources. I use a bucket policy to enforce the required access conditions and grant only the approved principals where necessary. Lifecycle rules control transition or expiration of objects and versions based on the organization's retention requirements, not simply a fixed arbitrary age. I review the plan for existing data impact and verify the access and lifecycle settings after apply.

094How do you create an Amazon ECR repository with image scanning, tag immutability and lifecycle policies?

ECR enhanced scanning may be configured at registry level. The example demonstrates repository basic scan-on-push; review the organization scanning mode and lifecycle preview.

HCL — ECR repository, basic scanning and lifecycle
resource "aws_ecr_repository" "app" {
  name                 = "payment-api"
  image_tag_mutability = "IMMUTABLE"
  encryption_configuration {
    encryption_type = "AES256"
  }
  image_scanning_configuration {
    scan_on_push = true
  }
}
resource "aws_ecr_lifecycle_policy" "app" {
  repository = aws_ecr_repository.app.name
  policy = jsonencode({
    rules = [{
      rulePriority = 1
      description  = "Expire old untagged images after 30 days"
      selection = {
        tagStatus   = "untagged"
        countType   = "sinceImagePushed"
        countUnit   = "days"
        countNumber = 30
      }
      action = { type = "expire" }
    }]
  })
}
output "repository_url" {
  value = aws_ecr_repository.app.repository_url
}
Terminal — example commands
# Preview retention policy against existing image inventory before deployment.
aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names payment-api
aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name payment-api

Final interview answer

I define an aws_ecr_repository resource for each independently versioned application, with approved encryption and tag mutability settings. I configure the applicable image scanning policy and a lifecycle policy that matches build frequency, release retention and rollback requirements. The CI role receives the required push permissions, while the deployment identity receives pull permissions. Before enabling expiration, I review its effect on live and rollback images because deleting a required image can prevent a later deployment from starting.

095How do you create an Amazon EKS cluster, managed node groups, IAM roles and required EKS add-ons using Terraform?

Example uses EC2 managed nodes, private endpoint access and a supported EKS cluster IAM role. The deployment runner needs private API connectivity and approved Kubernetes access. Review add-on compatibility before pinning versions.

HCL — EKS control plane, managed nodes and add-on pattern (identity and access prerequisites required)
# Declare inputs: cluster_name, cluster_version, private_subnet_ids,
# approved_instance_types, and IAM role ARNs for add-ons as appropriate.
resource "aws_iam_role" "cluster" {
  name = "${var.cluster_name}-cluster"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect = "Allow"
      Action = "sts:AssumeRole"
      Principal = { Service = "eks.amazonaws.com" }
    }]
  })
}
resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "cluster" {
  role       = aws_iam_role.cluster.name
  policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonEKSClusterPolicy"
}
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  name     = var.cluster_name
  version  = var.cluster_version
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.cluster.arn
  vpc_config {
    subnet_ids              = var.private_subnet_ids
    endpoint_private_access = true
    endpoint_public_access  = false
  }
  access_config {
    authentication_mode = "API"
  }
  depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.cluster]
}
resource "aws_iam_role" "node" {
  name = "${var.cluster_name}-nodes"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect = "Allow"
      Action = "sts:AssumeRole"
      Principal = { Service = "ec2.amazonaws.com" }
    }]
  })
}
resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "nodes" {
  for_each = toset([
    "AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy",
    "AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly"
  ])
  role       = aws_iam_role.node.name
  policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/${each.key}"
}
resource "aws_eks_node_group" "app" {
  cluster_name    = aws_eks_cluster.main.name
  node_group_name = "application"
  node_role_arn   = aws_iam_role.node.arn
  subnet_ids      = var.private_subnet_ids
  instance_types  = var.approved_instance_types
  scaling_config {
    min_size     = 2
    max_size     = 6
    desired_size = 2
  }
  depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.nodes]
}
# Configure a dedicated CNI workload role/identity with required permissions.
# Configure the EBS CSI driver identity separately if persistent EBS is needed.
resource "aws_eks_addon" "platform" {
  for_each     = var.approved_addon_versions
  cluster_name = aws_eks_cluster.main.name
  addon_name   = each.key
  addon_version = each.value
  # For addons requiring AWS permissions, configure the appropriate
  # workload identity or service_account_role_arn as supported.
  depends_on = [aws_eks_node_group.app]
}

For a complete deployment, bootstrap CNI permissions before nodes depend on them, configure compatible add-on creation ordering and EKS access entries, and provide NAT or private endpoints as required. A reviewed EKS module often handles these dependencies more reliably than a minimal interview excerpt.

Terminal — example commands
aws eks describe-cluster --name "$CLUSTER_NAME" --region ap-south-1
aws eks list-nodegroups --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" --region ap-south-1
aws eks list-addons --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" --region ap-south-1
# From an authorized runner with private endpoint reachability:
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name "$CLUSTER_NAME" --region ap-south-1
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system

Implementation / troubleshooting sequence

  1. Confirm AWS account, region, EKS version, CIDRs, endpoint access and supported subnets.
  2. Provision approved cluster and node IAM roles; configure CNI and other add-on workload identities.
  3. Create cluster, access entries, managed nodes and compatible add-ons in supported order.
  4. From an authorized private-network runner, verify cluster status, nodes and system workloads.

Final interview answer

I first prepare the VPC, suitable subnets and IAM roles needed for the EKS control plane and managed node groups. I define the cluster with the required endpoint access and version, then provision managed node groups with approved instance types, capacity and node placement. I configure compatible platform add-ons such as the VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy and required CSI drivers, along with their authorized identities. Once the cluster is active, I verify access using AWS CLI and kubectl and confirm node readiness and add-on health before handing it over for application deployment.

096How do you create Route 53 DNS records and configure an ACM certificate using Terraform?

An ALB certificate must be in the same region as the ALB. CloudFront certificates have different region requirements. The DNS validation record must be in the authorized zone.

HCL — Route 53 and ACM validation (required inputs declared separately)
data "aws_route53_zone" "public" {
  name         = var.zone_name
  private_zone = false
}
resource "aws_acm_certificate" "app" {
  domain_name       = var.app_domain
  validation_method = "DNS"
  lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }
}
resource "aws_route53_record" "validation" {
  for_each = {
    for dvo in aws_acm_certificate.app.domain_validation_options :
    dvo.domain_name => {
      name   = dvo.resource_record_name
      record = dvo.resource_record_value
      type   = dvo.resource_record_type
    }
  }
  zone_id = data.aws_route53_zone.public.zone_id
  name    = each.value.name
  type    = each.value.type
  ttl     = 60
  records = [each.value.record]
}
resource "aws_acm_certificate_validation" "app" {
  certificate_arn = aws_acm_certificate.app.arn
  validation_record_fqdns = [
    for record in aws_route53_record.validation : record.fqdn
  ]
}
resource "aws_route53_record" "app" {
  zone_id = data.aws_route53_zone.public.zone_id
  name    = var.app_domain
  type    = "A"
  alias {
    name                   = var.alb_dns_name
    zone_id                = var.alb_zone_id
    evaluate_target_health = true
  }
}
# Reference aws_acm_certificate_validation.app.certificate_arn
# in the HTTPS listener so validation is completed first.
Terminal — example commands
dig +short "$APP_DOMAIN"
aws acm describe-certificate --certificate-arn "$CERTIFICATE_ARN"
curl --fail --show-error "https://$APP_DOMAIN/health"

Final interview answer

I start by identifying the authorized Route 53 hosted zone and the application domain name. I request an ACM certificate in the appropriate region, create the DNS validation record using the certificate's domain validation options and wait for validation before using the certificate on an HTTPS listener. I create a Route 53 alias record pointing to the approved ALB or other supported target. Finally, I verify DNS resolution and HTTPS connectivity, including the certificate hostname and listener configuration.

097How do you automatically configure an EC2 instance after provisioning using Terraform user_data and cloud-init?

User data normally runs at initial instance boot according to cloud-init configuration. Changes to user data do not guarantee that an existing machine reruns the script.

HCL — render EC2 initialization data
# Within an approved aws_instance resource:
# user_data = templatefile("${path.module}/user_data.tftpl", {
#   app_name = "payment-api"
# })
# Do not include credentials in the template.
cloud-init — user_data.tftpl (example Ubuntu AMI)
#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages:
  - nginx
write_files:
  - path: /var/www/html/index.html
    content: "Provisioned with Terraform: ${app_name}"
runcmd:
  - [systemctl, enable, --now, nginx]
Terminal — example commands
# On the authorized EC2 instance:
cloud-init status --long
sudo journalctl -u cloud-final --no-pager
sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/cloud-init-output.log
curl --fail http://localhost/

Final interview answer

I use EC2 user_data to pass an approved initialization script or cloud-init configuration at instance launch. Terraform can render the script using templatefile with environment-specific nonsecret values, such as the application name or configuration location. I make the script safe to rerun where appropriate and retrieve sensitive information using an authorized runtime role instead of embedding credentials in user data. After provisioning, I inspect cloud-init status and logs and verify the required service has actually started.

TerraformTerragrunt

Terragrunt is a wrapper and orchestration tool that helps teams organize and run Terraform or compatible IaC configurations. It can centralize repeated settings, coordinate dependencies between infrastructure units and make environment-specific configurations easier to maintain. Terraform is still responsible for planning and applying the infrastructure through providers and state. I would consider Terragrunt when a large multi-account repository has significant repeated configuration or dependency orchestration needs, but for a smaller project plain Terraform roots and modules may be simpler.

099What is the difference between TFLint, Checkov and Terraform Validate? How do you use them to improve Terraform code quality and security?
FeatureTerraform ValidateTFLintCheckov
PurposeConfiguration consistencyLint and provider rulesIaC security and policy scanning
Typical findingInvalid resource argumentUnused declaration or provider-specific issueUnrestricted ingress or missing security control
Runs afterProvider/module initializationTFLint plugin initializationConfiguration checkout
Commandterraform validatetflint --recursivecheckov -d .
Does not replacePlan or testsPlan or security reviewRuntime security or human review
CLI · standard CI checks (tools installed)
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
tflint --init
tflint --recursive
checkov -d .

Final interview answer

Terraform validate checks the syntax and internal consistency of Terraform configuration using installed provider schemas. TFLint adds linting rules that can identify style, unused declarations and provider-specific problems depending on its plugins. Checkov performs infrastructure-as-code security and policy scanning to identify configurations that may violate approved standards, such as an unrestricted security group. I run these as separate CI checks and review their findings before plan, because none of them alone guarantees that an AWS deployment will be secure or successful.

100What is HCP Terraform (formerly Terraform Cloud), and how is it different from running Terraform locally or through Jenkins?
FeatureLocal Terraform CLIJenkinsHCP Terraform
ExecutionDeveloper workstationSelf-managed CI agentConfigured remote or supported execution mode
StateConfigured backendConfigured backendManaged workspace state where used
CredentialsLocal authorized profileCI credential or roleWorkspace/agent identity mechanisms
ApprovalsProcess must be establishedPipeline gatesPlatform run controls depending on setup
OperationsEngineer manages environmentTeam operates JenkinsManaged platform capabilities

HCP Terraform workspaces are not the same concept as Terraform CLI workspaces; they can have their own execution settings and state.

Final interview answer

HCP Terraform is a managed platform for Terraform workflows that can provide centralized state, remote execution, collaboration, policy checks and run history depending on configuration and entitlement. A local CLI workflow runs on an engineer's machine, while Jenkins can run Terraform through a self-managed pipeline and requires us to build the surrounding approvals, credentials, state and operational controls. I choose based on organizational governance, existing CI integration, execution requirements and cost. Regardless of the runner, the infrastructure code, provider versions, target identity and approved plan must remain controlled.

109Once you receive an infrastructure provisioning ticket, what steps do you follow from requirement gathering to deployment and ticket closure?

Illustrative project answer — adapt the details, counts and responsibilities to your actual experience.

Do not close a ticket simply because terraform apply succeeded. Verify the acceptance criteria, actual configuration, access and application functionality as applicable.

Implementation / troubleshooting sequence

  1. Read the Jira request and clarify missing technical/security requirements with the requesting team.
  2. Select the proper root and approved modules, then create a feature branch.
  3. Run formatting, validation, security checks and generate the environment plan.
  4. Review the PR and obtain exact-plan deployment approval.
  5. Apply through the trusted pipeline, verify actual AWS settings and acceptance criteria, record evidence and close the ticket.

Final interview answer

After receiving the ticket, I review the requirements with the requesting team and confirm the target environment, dependencies and acceptance criteria. I create a feature branch, update the appropriate Terraform modules or root configuration and run formatting, validation and security checks. I review the Terraform plan through a pull request, obtain the necessary approvals and apply the reviewed changes through our authorized pipeline. Finally, I verify the actual AWS resources and application connectivity, attach nonsecret evidence and the PR reference to the ticket, and close it after the requester confirms the requirement is satisfied.

CI/CD and DevSecOps — Advanced

116Explain your complete Terraform CI/CD pipeline, from GitHub code commit to production infrastructure provisioning.

Illustrative project answer — adapt the details, counts and responsibilities to your actual experience.

Pipeline stagePurpose
CheckoutApproved Git revision
fmt and validateConfiguration quality
TFLint and CheckovLinting and security controls
TestsValidate expected module behavior
AuthenticateScoped AWS identity and state access
PlanSave exact proposed changes
ApprovalReview plan and change request
ApplyApply reviewed artifact with locking
VerifyConfirm infrastructure and acceptance criteria
Terminal — example commands
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform init -lockfile=readonly
terraform validate
tflint --init && tflint --recursive
checkov -d .
# Run approved tests in the designated environment.
